title: How to Get People to Pay You (Free, No Audience)
channel: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
promo_conflict: Caleb promotes businesses he owns, including a direct $10/month Post For Me offer; performance metrics are self-reported.

idea.name: Post For Me
idea.one_liner: A subscription SaaS for developers and product teams to add social media posting and integrations to their apps.
idea.customer: Technical users, developers, and SaaS or product teams that want social posting integrations.
idea.offer: Social media posting software and integrations, with customer support and help resources.
idea.revenue_model: Monthly subscription plans, starting at $10/month, with higher tiers at $25, $50, and $100/month.

key_quotes.quote: So they came up with an idea for an app that can help people post their content to social media.
There's a bunch of apps that do this, but this app is pointed towards more technical people, developers, and that wasn't really being done.
And these articles are really specific to how to achieve this one specific goal based on this one specific problem.
We integrated a chat bot into our website and we turned off all of the AI features.

claims.claim: The guest said the business's monthly recurring revenue exceeded his previous salary.
claims.quote: monthly recurring revenue exceeded any salary that I had up until this point.

claims.claim: They started running Google Ads after crossing $10,000 in monthly recurring revenue.
claims.quote: We just now started running Google ads after we crossed 10,000.

claims.claim: The launch tweet got about 200 views.
claims.quote: That tweet got about 200 views.

claims.claim: The host said MRR rose from $300 to $500, reaching $500 after five months.
claims.quote: $300 monthly recurring revenue, then 500. In fact, after five months, they had $500 in monthly recurring revenue, but they were stoked about this.

claims.claim: The guest said the company was nearing $500 MRR.
claims.quote: And I said, well, let's check and we were closing in on $500 in monthly recurring.

claims.claim: The guest said the product cost $10/month and nearly 50 people wanted to use it.
claims.quote: I was like, wow, this isn't saying, you know, at 10 bucks a month. I was like, almost 50 people want to use something that I built.

claims.claim: They celebrated each additional $100 in MRR by doing an extra push-up.
claims.quote: And so my wife and I made a deal for every $100 of monthly recurring that we added.

claims.claim: The host said the guest had about 1,200 Twitter followers and that Twitter was still bringing business.
claims.quote: Even to this day, he has like 1200 followers, but it's still driving him a ton of business.

claims.claim: The host said the guest had 500 Twitter followers when he began posting MRR updates.
claims.quote: I'm just going to post screenshots to Twitter to my, at the time, 500 Twitter followers, which is the average that most people have on Twitter.

claims.claim: One tweet received 24,000 impressions.
claims.quote: So we ended up getting 24,000 impressions.

claims.claim: That tweet received 114 replies.
claims.quote: The biggest surprise to me was the 114 replies.

claims.claim: The host described the tweet's engagement rate as 6.4%.
claims.quote: man, 6.4% engagement rate, super good.

claims.claim: The guest said the product passed $5,000 MRR within eight months.
claims.quote: I can't believe that we built the product and grew it to over 5K in eight months.

claims.claim: The host said a later post got a thousand times more views than an earlier one.
claims.quote: Got a hundred times more, actually, sorry, a thousand times more views.

claims.claim: The guest said he posted an update for every additional $500 in MRR.
claims.quote: And I mean, you could even see in some of the other posts, like for example, I was posting every 500 in MRR.

claims.claim: They were adding between $500 and $1,000 in MRR week over week.
claims.quote: And so at that point in time, we were seeing anywhere between 500 to $1,000 in monthly recurring being added week over week.

claims.claim: MRR grew from $4,500 to $5,000 in five days.
claims.quote: So like the jump from 4,500 to 5,000 only took us five days.

claims.claim: The guest said the SEO strategy had improved around the time they reached $2,000 MRR.
claims.quote: I think it was about the time that we hit $2,000 in monthly recurring that our search engine optimization, kind of our strategy for organic marketing had gotten really, really good.

claims.claim: The founders provided round-the-clock customer chat coverage.
claims.quote: So we did 24 seven coverage, but it was really, we were really, really adamant to always being available on our phones or on a computer

claims.claim: They noted customer problems when they encountered the same problem at least twice.
claims.quote: anytime we noticed that a problem was felt by one of our customers at least twice

claims.claim: The host estimated one reported problem could represent 10 to 30 other people with the same issue.
claims.quote: That means that they probably represent 10 to 30 more people that are not bothering to go out of their way.

claims.claim: The cofounder published at least one help article a week, sometimes two or three.
claims.quote: And then, yeah, early on this year, he was posting, you know, a minimum of one per week, and sometimes, you know, two, three of them per week.

claims.claim: Their best week added about $1,000 in MRR.
claims.quote: I think the best week, if I remember correctly, the best week that we had was like $1,000 in MRR in one week

claims.claim: Their lowest reported churn was 10%.
claims.quote: The lowest our churn was at was 10%.

claims.claim: Churn rose from 13% to 16% and then above 17%.
claims.quote: First hit, you know, 13%, and then 16%. Now it's at over 17%.

claims.claim: They were 10 to 11 months into the business when they began investing heavily in analytics.
claims.quote: So now we are at the point, you know, 10, 11 months in where we are investing really heavily in telemetry and metrics in analytics.

claims.claim: The entry plan was $10/month with unlimited scaling on the pricing model.
claims.quote: So we start at $10 a month, but you can scale unlimited on our pricing model.

claims.claim: They were guiding their first customers through upgrades to $25, $50, and $100 plans.
claims.quote: And we are within these last couple of months walking our first set of customers through the process of upgrading to, you know, a $25 plan, a $50 plan, a $100 plan.

claims.claim: The guest advertised a $10/month plan.
claims.quote: the fastest, easiest, most scalable, cheapest way to do it is to go to post for me.dev and get started with our $10 a month plan.

acquisition_channels.details: The founder posted MRR screenshots and milestones on Twitter and replied to people who engaged.
They published help articles from customer problems, improved site metadata, and reported referrals from search engines and LLMs.
They began testing Google Ads after crossing $10,000 MRR.

ideas.delivery: Customers use the SaaS and its social media integrations in their apps. The founders initially handled support chat themselves around the clock and created help articles from recurring customer questions.
ideas.other_uk_rules: Potential UK GDPR obligations for account and connected social data; DMCC Act subscription rules may apply if sold to UK consumers.

stated_problem.quote: I don't have the time or the ability to build a product myself, but I'd love for you guys to build a product.
stated_problem.speaker: Caleb Panza

idea.name: Damon Development
idea.one_liner: A software and digital services agency that builds client products and provides design, marketing, and website work for project fees.
idea.customer: Founders and businesses that need a product or digital work built, including physical service businesses.
idea.offer: Custom software development, design, marketing, WordPress website updates, and Webflow sites; some work was outsourced.
idea.revenue_model: Client fees for development and related project work; prices are not stated.

key_quotes.quote: Our software company is called Damon Development.
We were saying yes to updating WordPress websites, building out web flow sites
It took us two years of working on other people stuff

claims.claim: The founders spent two years working on other people's projects before building products.
claims.quote: It took us two years of working on other people stuff

acquisition_channels.details: The guest invited prospective customers to schedule a call through Damon.dev; no other acquisition method is stated.

ideas.delivery: The founders provide software, design, and marketing work to clients, sometimes outsourcing parts of projects; prospective customers can schedule a call with Caleb.
ideas.other_uk_rules: UK GDPR may apply when handling client or end-user data. No worker placement service is described.
